claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis presented in Supplementary file 4.

claims.claim: The histone acetyltranferases Gcn5 and Mst2 negatively regulate silencing of the ST domains at the termini of chromosomes I and II.
claims.source: Intriguingly, the histone acetyltranferases Gcn5 and Mst2 also negatively regulate silencing of the ST domains at the termini of chromosomes I and II (Gómez et al., 2005; Nugent et al., 2010; Figure 4D, data re-analyzed from Nugent et al., 2010), and by RT-PCR analysis of fah1+ and grt1+ expression, we confirmed downregulation of ST gene expression in gcn5Δmst2Δ cells (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature and data presented in Figure 4D and E.

claims.claim: Downregulation of ST gene expression was confirmed in gcn5Δmst2Δ cells.
claims.source: Intriguingly, the histone acetyltranferases Gcn5 and Mst2 also negatively regulate silencing of the ST domains at the termini of chromosomes I and II (Gómez et al., 2005; Nugent et al., 2010; Figure 4D, data re-analyzed from Nugent et al., 2010), and by RT-PCR analysis of fah1+ and grt1+ expression, we confirmed downregulation of ST gene expression in gcn5Δmst2Δ cells (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The downregulation of subtelomeric regions in G34R cells in which K36 acetylation is reduced is mirrored in cells lacking H3 K36 acetyltransferase function.
claims.source: Thus the downregulation of subtelomeric regions in G34R cells in which K36 acetylation is reduced is mirrored in cells lacking H3 K36 acetyltransferase function.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing G34R and gcn5Δmst2Δ cells.

claims.claim: Subtelomeric domains are the most highly condensed regions of fission yeast chromatin and are microscopically visible as DAPI-stained 'knobs'.
claims.source: Subtelomeric domains are surprisingly the most highly condensed regions of fission yeast chromatin and are microscopically visible as DAPI (4',6-diamidino-2-phenylindole)-stained 'knobs' (Matsuda et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: Knob formation correlates with transcriptional silencing within subtelomeric domains.
claims.source: Knob formation correlates with transcriptional silencing within subtelomeric domains, and requires Set2 H3K36 methyltransferase and the Shugoshin protein (Sgo2; Matsuda et al., 2015; Tashiro et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: Knob formation requires Set2 H3K36 methyltransferase and the Shugoshin protein (Sgo2).
claims.source: Knob formation correlates with transcriptional silencing within subtelomeric domains, and requires Set2 H3K36 methyltransferase and the Shugoshin protein (Sgo2; Matsuda et al., 2015; Tashiro et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: Sgo2 is an important component of the tension-sensing machinery that assembles at centromeres during mitosis.
claims.source: Sgo2 is an important component of the tension-sensing machinery that assembles at centromeres during mitosis and relays turn-off of the mitotic checkpoint once kinetochores have properly attached to spindle microtubules (Watanabe, 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: Sgo2 has been found at subtelomeres in interphase cells, where it promotes silencing, and regulates timing of replication of ST domains.
claims.source: Recently however Sgo2 has been found at subtelomeres in interphase cells, where it promotes silencing, and regulates timing of replication of ST domains (Tashiro et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: The proportion of cells with visible knobs and their number per cell was significantly elevated in H3-G34R but not in H3-G34V cells.
claims.source: Notably, the proportion of cells with visible knobs and their number per cell was significantly elevated in H3-G34R but not in H3-G34V cells (Figure 5A), and as expected, knobs were reduced in cells lacking Set2 (Matsuda et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Knobs were reduced in cells lacking Set2.
claims.source: Notably, the proportion of cells with visible knobs and their number per cell was significantly elevated in H3-G34R but not in H3-G34V cells (Figure 5A), and as expected, knobs were reduced in cells lacking Set2 (Matsuda et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to published literature.

claims.claim: H3-K36Q mutant cells that mimic H3K36 acetylation and block K36 methylation dramatically loose knobs.
claims.source: A previous study showed that H3-K36Q mutant cells that mimic H3K36 acetylation and block K36 methylation dramatically loose knobs (Matsuda et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: Knob formation in gcn5Δmst2Δ mutants is elevated, similar to levels in the K36ac-deficient H3-G34R cells.
claims.source: Indeed knob formation in gcn5Δmst2Δ mutants is elevated, similar to levels in the K36ac-deficient H3-G34R cells (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Sgo2-FLAG is significantly enriched at ST domains in H3-G34R cells compared with H3-G34V or H3-WT.
claims.source: Indeed ChIP revealed Sgo2-FLAG to be significantly enriched at ST domains in H3-G34R cells compared with H3-G34V or H3-WT (Figure 5C), and that Sgo2 is highly enriched at ST domains in mst2Δgcn5Δ relative to WT controls (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Sgo2 is highly enriched at ST domains in mst2Δgcn5Δ relative to WT controls.
claims.source: Indeed ChIP revealed Sgo2-FLAG to be significantly enriched at ST domains in H3-G34R cells compared with H3-G34V or H3-WT (Figure 5C), and that Sgo2 is highly enriched at ST domains in mst2Δgcn5Δ relative to WT controls (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Sgo2 normally accumulates at centromeres in mitosis and is recruited to ST in interphase.
claims.source: Since Sgo2 normally accumulates at centromeres in mitosis and is recruited to ST in interphase (Kawashima et al., 2010; Matsuda et al., 2015; Tashiro et al., 2016), we asked whether H3-G34R influences the cell cycle dependence of its localization.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: Sgo2 accumulation at centromeres in mitosis was unaffected by H3-G34R mutation.
claims.source: Importantly, Sgo2 accumulation at centromeres in mitosis was unaffected by H3-G34R mutation (Figure 5E), but even in mitotically arrested cells, Sgo2 was preferentially enriched at ST domains in H3-G34R cells compared with H3-WT (Figure 5F), suggestive that in H3-G34R cells, cell cycle regulation of Sgo2 accumulation at ST is perturbed.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Even in mitotically arrested cells, Sgo2 was preferentially enriched at ST domains in H3-G34R cells compared with H3-WT.
claims.source: Importantly, Sgo2 accumulation at centromeres in mitosis was unaffected by H3-G34R mutation (Figure 5E), but even in mitotically arrested cells, Sgo2 was preferentially enriched at ST domains in H3-G34R cells compared with H3-WT (Figure 5F), suggestive that in H3-G34R cells, cell cycle regulation of Sgo2 accumulation at ST is perturbed.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: In H3-G34R cells, cell cycle regulation of Sgo2 accumulation at ST is perturbed.
claims.source: Importantly, Sgo2 accumulation at centromeres in mitosis was unaffected by H3-G34R mutation (Figure 5E), but even in mitotically arrested cells, Sgo2 was preferentially enriched at ST domains in H3-G34R cells compared with H3-WT (Figure 5F), suggestive that in H3-G34R cells, cell cycle regulation of Sgo2 accumulation at ST is perturbed.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 5E and F.

claims.claim: Sgo2 accumulates at subtelomeres in H3-G34R or H3K36ac-deficient cells, correlating with enhanced silencing of ST domains and knob formation in these cells.
claims.source: In summary, our data suggest that Sgo2 accumulates at subtelomeres in H3-G34R or H3K36ac-deficient cells, correlating with enhanced silencing of ST domains and knob formation in these cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claims.claim: H3-G34K cells had elevated Sgo2 at ST sites.
claims.source: We also performed Sgo2 ChIP in H3-G34K cells. Consistent with enhanced Sgo2 recruitment to silenced ST domains seen in H3K36ac acetyltransferase defective and H3-G34R strains, H3-G34K cells also had elevated Sgo2 at ST sites (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: There was no change in H3K36me3 in mixed copy H3-G34R, H3-G34V, or H3-G34K strains compared with 3xH3 WT.
claims.source: We first asked if H3K36me3 was reduced in mixed H3 strains and found no change in H3K36me3 in mixed copy H3-G34R, H3-G34V, or H3-G34K strains compared with 3xH3 WT (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: There was no dominant increase in levels of H3K36me2 when the mutants were expressed in mixed H3 backgrounds.
claims.source: Similarly, we found no dominant increase in levels of H3K36me2 when the mutants were expressed in mixed H3 backgrounds (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: These results are consistent with the lack of dominant effect of G34R or G34V mutations on K36 methylation in mammalian cells.
claims.source: These results are consistent with the lack of dominant effect of G34R or G34V mutations on K36 methylation in mammalian cells (Lewis et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: Loss of H3K36ac was restricted to the G34R mutant H3 protein in mixed copy H3-G34R strain.
claims.source: We found that loss of H3K36ac was restricted to the G34R mutant H3 protein, whereas K36ac was present at comparable levels on wild-type H3 purified from the mixed copy G34R and wild-type 3xH3 strains (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: K36ac was present at comparable levels on wild-type H3 purified from the mixed copy G34R and wild-type 3xH3 strains.
claims.source: We found that loss of H3K36ac was restricted to the G34R mutant H3 protein, whereas K36ac was present at comparable levels on wild-type H3 purified from the mixed copy G34R and wild-type 3xH3 strains (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Mixed copy strains grew as well as 3xH3 WT strains, with the notable exception of H3-G34R (3xH3), which like the sole copy H3-G34R mutant, grew less well in the presence of HU.
claims.source: Mixed copy strains grew as well as 3xH3 WT strains, with the notable exception of H3-G34R (3xH3), which like the sole copy H3-G34R mutant, grew less well in the presence of HU (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: H3-G34K and H3-G34V mixed copy strains grew as well as WT (3xH3) strains on bleomycin and zeocin.
claims.source: We also tested sensitivity to IR mimetics, and found that H3-G34K and H3-G34V mixed copy strains grew as well as WT (3xH3) strains on bleomycin and zeocin (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: There was no evidence of increased chromosome loss in the mixed H3 backgrounds for either H3-G34K or H3-G34R.
claims.source: In contrast to the chromosome missegregation seen in H3-G34R and H3-G34K sole copy strains, there was no evidence of increased chromosome loss in the mixed H3 backgrounds for either H3-G34K or H3-G34R (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: There was a significant drop in efficiency for H3-G34R mixed copy strains in the plasmid-based HR DNA repair assay.
claims.source: There was however a significant drop in efficiency for H3-G34R mixed copy strains in our plasmid-based HR DNA repair assay (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: The overall numbers of genes that are differentially expressed in the (3xH3) background are reduced compared with the number of differentially regulated genes in the sole copy strains.
claims.source: We note that the overall numbers of genes that are differentially expressed in the (3xH3) background are reduced compared with the number of differentially regulated genes in the sole copy strains (54 genes differentially expressed in H3-G34R (3xH3) vs 160 genes in H3-G34R, and 142 genes differentially expressed in H3-G34K (3xH3) vs 223 in H3-G34K when using FDR 5% and FC of 1.5), suggestive that the presence of wild-type H3 partially overrides some transcriptional effects of the mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: The presence of wild-type H3 partially overrides some transcriptional effects of the mutants.
claims.source: We note that the overall numbers of genes that are differentially expressed in the (3xH3) background are reduced compared with the number of differentially regulated genes in the sole copy strains (54 genes differentially expressed in H3-G34R (3xH3) vs 160 genes in H3-G34R, and 142 genes differentially expressed in H3-G34K (3xH3) vs 223 in H3-G34K when using FDR 5% and FC of 1.5), suggestive that the presence of wild-type H3 partially overrides some transcriptional effects of the mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from RNA-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: The majority of genes influenced by mutation in the (3xH3) background were also differentially regulated in the sole copy backgrounds.
claims.source: Using the more relaxed criteria of p<0.05, we found that the majority of genes influenced by mutation in the (3xH3) background were also differentially regulated in the sole copy backgrounds (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 4.

claims.claim: Subtelomeric domains of chromosomes I and II were repressed in H3-G34R mixed copy strains compared with WT H3 (3xH3).
claims.source: Manhattan plots indicated that subtelomeric domains of chromosomes I and II were repressed in H3-G34R mixed copy strains compared with WT H3 (3xH3), with a similar, but less marked trend also in H3-G34K mixed copy strains (Figure 6G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: A similar, but less marked trend of ST domain repression was also seen in H3-G34K mixed copy strains.
claims.source: Manhattan plots indicated that subtelomeric domains of chromosomes I and II were repressed in H3-G34R mixed copy strains compared with WT H3 (3xH3), with a similar, but less marked trend also in H3-G34K mixed copy strains (Figure 6G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: A high proportion of genes repressed in G34R and G34K mixed copy strains were resident within ST domains (10/30 and 25/69, respectively).
claims.source: Extending this analysis to ask if subtelomeric domains were preferentially repressed in H3-G34R or H3-G34K mixed copy strains (using FDR 5% and FC of 1.5), we found that a high proportion of genes repressed in G34R and G34K mixed copy strains were resident with ST domains (10/30 and 25/69, respectively) compared with only 1/24 and 7/73 of genes activated in G34R and G34K mixed copy strains (Supplemental Table S4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis presented in Supplementary file 4.

claims.claim: Only 1/24 and 7/73 of genes activated in G34R and G34K mixed copy strains were resident within ST domains.
claims.source: Extending this analysis to ask if subtelomeric domains were preferentially repressed in H3-G34R or H3-G34K mixed copy strains (using FDR 5% and FC of 1.5), we found that a high proportion of genes repressed in G34R and G34K mixed copy strains were resident with ST domains (10/30 and 25/69, respectively) compared with only 1/24 and 7/73 of genes activated in G34R and G34K mixed copy strains (Supplemental Table S4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis presented in Supplementary file 4.

claims.claim: Many of the genes that are repressed by the H3-G34R or G34K mutation are situated in ST domains of chromosomes I and II.
claims.source: Thus many of the genes that are repressed by the H3-G34R or G34K mutation are situated in ST domains of chromosomes I and II, and the hyper-repression of gene expression within ST domains is dominant since it is evident in the mixed copy background strains.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: The hyper-repression of gene expression within ST domains is dominant since it is evident in the mixed copy background strains.
claims.source: Thus many of the genes that are repressed by the H3-G34R or G34K mutation are situated in ST domains of chromosomes I and II, and the hyper-repression of gene expression within ST domains is dominant since it is evident in the mixed copy background strains.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from RNA-seq data comparing sole copy and mixed copy strains.

claims.claim: Activity of the H3K36 tri-methylase SETD2 is blocked on nucleosomes bearing H3.3 G34 mutations.
claims.source: However, consistent with a defect in tri-methylation, a very recent report shows that activity of the H3K36 tri-methylase SETD2 is blocked on nucleosomes bearing H3.3 G34 mutations, whereas NSD2-mediated di-methylation is unaffected (Jain et al., 2020), although in that study, G34R, G34V, and G34W similarly affected tri-methylation, whereas we saw no defect in H3K36me3 in the H3-G34W mutant, or H3-G34M, or G34Q strains.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: NSD2-mediated di-methylation is unaffected on nucleosomes bearing H3.3 G34 mutations.
claims.source: However, consistent with a defect in tri-methylation, a very recent report shows that activity of the H3K36 tri-methylase SETD2 is blocked on nucleosomes bearing H3.3 G34 mutations, whereas NSD2-mediated di-methylation is unaffected (Jain et al., 2020), although in that study, G34R, G34V, and G34W similarly affected tri-methylation, whereas we saw no defect in H3K36me3 in the H3-G34W mutant, or H3-G34M, or G34Q strains.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: Fission yeast H3 differs from H3.3 at several residues including alanines instead of serines at residues 28 and 31 within the H3 tail.
claims.source: Another possibility is that the differences in K36me3 stem from our analysis of fission yeast H3, which differs from H3.3 at several residues including alanines instead of serines at residues 28 and 31 within the H3 tail (Matsumoto and Yanagida, 1985; Yadav et al., 2017), which may influence K36 methyltransferase behavior on G34 mutant templates (Schuhmacher et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: Co-expression of mutant (H3-G34R, V, or K) with wild-type H3 proteins did not affect H3K36me3.
claims.source: However, consistent with previous studies in mammalian cells, we found that co-expression of mutant (H3-G34R, V, or K) with wild-type H3 proteins did not affect H3K36me3, suggesting that if indeed Set2 activity is altered, loss of Set2-mediated trimethylation of K36 is limited to the mutant H3 tail.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: If Set2 activity is altered, loss of Set2-mediated trimethylation of K36 is limited to the mutant H3 tail.
claims.source: However, consistent with previous studies in mammalian cells, we found that co-expression of mutant (H3-G34R, V, or K) with wild-type H3 proteins did not affect H3K36me3, suggesting that if indeed Set2 activity is altered, loss of Set2-mediated trimethylation of K36 is limited to the mutant H3 tail.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claims.claim: In fission yeast, H3-G34R mutants with reduced K36ac and K36me3 are defective for HR-mediated repair of DNA breaks.
claims.source: K36 modifications have been linked to DNA damage response. In fission yeast, H3-G34R mutants with reduced K36ac and K36me3 are defective for HR-mediated repair of DNA breaks, whilst H3-G34V mutants, which maintain K36ac but have reduced K36me3, show no defect in HR.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: H3-G34V mutants, which maintain K36ac but have reduced K36me3, show no defect in HR.
claims.source: K36 modifications have been linked to DNA damage response. In fission yeast, H3-G34R mutants with reduced K36ac and K36me3 are defective for HR-mediated repair of DNA breaks, whilst H3-G34V mutants, which maintain K36ac but have reduced K36me3, show no defect in HR.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Reduction in K36me3 is not causal of the HR defect.
claims.source: Since both mutants (and HR-proficient H3-G34K) have reduced H3K36me3, reduction in K36me3 is not causal of the HR defect.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing different mutants.

claims.claim: Gcn5 mutants are reduced for H3K36ac, are HU sensitive, and are also defective for HR.
claims.source: However, like H3-G34R mutants, Gcn5 mutants are reduced for H3K36ac, are HU sensitive, and are also defective for HR (Pai et al., 2014); so these phenotypes may be linked.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: Gcn5 is the major H3K36 acetyltransferase in fission yeast.
claims.source: We confirmed that Gcn5 is the major H3K36 acetyltransferase in fission yeast and then showed in vitro that Gcn5 activity was lost specifically at K36 on recombinant G34R H3.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1E and 1F.

claims.claim: Gcn5 activity was lost specifically at K36 on recombinant G34R H3 in vitro.
claims.source: We confirmed that Gcn5 is the major H3K36 acetyltransferase in fission yeast and then showed in vitro that Gcn5 activity was lost specifically at K36 on recombinant G34R H3.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: H3-G34R directly affects Gcn5 function.
claims.source: This result emphasizes that H3-G34R directly affects Gcn5 function, but meant that we could not bypass the K36 acetylation defect in H3-G34R cells by Gcn5 overexpression to assign specific phenotypes to loss of H3K36ac.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing loss of Gcn5 activity on G34R H3.

claims.claim: It remains unclear whether the HR defect and sensitivity to HU seen in G34R cells are caused by loss of H3K36ac.
claims.source: It therefore remains unclear whether the HR defect and sensitivity to HU seen in G34R cells are caused by loss of H3K36ac.
claims.evidence: This claim acknowledges the limitation of the current data in establishing causality.

claims.claim: The histone mutants disrupt the local chromatin architecture such that deposition of H3-G34R at leu1 reduces local levels of K36ac and disrupts HR at that locus.
claims.source: However, since chromatin is assembled from nucleosomes bearing two copies of H3, one possibility is that even in the presence of excess WT H3, H3K36ac is sufficiently diluted to cause dominant defects in HR and dominant HU sensitivity. In other words, the histone mutants disrupt the local chromatin architecture such that deposition of H3-G34R at leu1 reduces local levels of K36ac and disrupts HR at that locus.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from experimental data.

claims.claim: Similar explanations have been suggested for local dominant roles of other histone mutants identified in cancer.
claims.source: Similar explanations have been suggested for local dominant roles of other histone mutants identified in cancer (Nacev et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: The unique phenotypes of H3-G34R mutants may be due to the generation of a novel site of arginine methylation within the H3 tail.
claims.source: Another possibility would be that the unique phenotypes of H3-G34R mutants are due to the generation of a novel site of arginine methylation within the H3 tail. We have used mass spectroscopy to explore this possibility, but found no evidence for methylation of H3-G34R in fission yeast (Lowe et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative but tested experimentally, with no evidence found for arginine methylation.

claims.claim: No evidence was found for methylation of H3-G34R in fission yeast.
claims.source: Another possibility would be that the unique phenotypes of H3-G34R mutants are due to the generation of a novel site of arginine methylation within the H3 tail. We have used mass spectroscopy to explore this possibility, but found no evidence for methylation of H3-G34R in fission yeast (Lowe et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to published work.

claims.claim: Local perturbation of chromatin structure from deposition of the mutant histones is insufficient to yield IR sensitivity in the presence of wild-type H3.
claims.source: In contrast to H3-G34R cells, which are not sensitive to γ-IR, both H3-G34V and H3-G34K are sensitive to γ-IR and to IR-mimetics but there was no dominant effect since mixed copy strains were not sensitive to IR mimetics. This may mean that local perturbation of chromatin structure from deposition of the mutant histones is insufficient to yield IR sensitivity in the presence of wild-type H3.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing sole copy and mixed copy strains.

claims.claim: Substitution of G34 with basic residues K or R led to accumulation of Sgo2 at subtelomeric (ST) domains correlating with enhanced silencing of these regions.

claims.claim: Cells defective for gcn5Δ and mst2Δ show repression of ST domains.
claims.source: Cells defective for gcn5Δ and mst2Δ similarly show repression of ST domains (Nugent et al., 2010), and we found that they accumulate Sgo2 at ST domains and, like G34R, accumulate knobs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature and experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claims.claim: At ST domains, Sgo2 controls the timing of replication of late replicating origins.
claims.source: At ST domains, Sgo2 controls the timing of replication of late replicating origins, and loss of Sgo2 advances replication of some ST origins (Tashiro et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: Loss of Sgo2 advances replication of some ST origins.
claims.source: At ST domains, Sgo2 controls the timing of replication of late replicating origins, and loss of Sgo2 advances replication of some ST origins (Tashiro et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: The elevated levels of Sgo2 at ST domains in H3-G34R, H3-G34K, and H3K36 acetyltransferase mutants may further delay the timing of late-replicating ST origins, leading to chromosome mis-segregation, as well as replicative stress sensitivity.
claims.source: One possibility is that the elevated levels of Sgo2 at ST domains in H3-G34R, H3-G34K, and H3K36 acetyltransferase mutants further delays the timing of late-replicating ST origins, leading to chromosome mis-segregation, as well as replicative stress sensitivity.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from experimental data and published literature.

claims.claim: The aberrant accumulation of Sgo2 at ST domains in mitotic H3-G34R cells could indirectly perturb centromere function.
claims.source: Alternately, the aberrant accumulation of Sgo2 at ST domains in mitotic H3-G34R cells could indirectly perturb centromere function. This is not due to depletion of Sgo2 from centromeres (as centromeric Sgo2 accumulation is similar between G34R and wild-type cells), but perhaps from mislocalization and/or depletion of a limiting factor that is normally recruited by Sgo2 to centromeres in mitosis, and that in G34R cells is now retargeted preferentially to ST domains.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from experimental data.

claims.claim: Silencing of ST domains is maintained in mixed copy strains, whereas chromosome missegregation is corrected.
claims.source: However, we note that silencing of ST domains is maintained in mixed copy strains, whereas chromosome missegregation is corrected.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Recruitment of Shugoshin proteins relies on Bub1 kinase-mediated phosphorylation of histone H2A on S121 (T120 in mammals).
claims.source: What is clear from many organisms is that recruitment of Shugoshin proteins relies on Bub1 kinase-mediated phosphorylation of histone H2A on S121 (T120 in mammals) (Kawashima et al., 2010; Kitajima et al., 2005; Kitajima et al., 2004; Matsuda et al., 2015; Tang et al., 2004; Tashiro et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: Both Bub1 kinase dead and H2A-S121A mutants lose localization of Sgo2 from centromeres and subtelomeres in fission yeast.
claims.source: In fission yeast, both Bub1 kinase dead and H2A-S121A mutants lose localization of Sgo2 from centromeres and subtelomeres (Tashiro et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: H3-G34R mutants alter the kinetics of phosphorylation at residues S128/129 of histone H2A.
claims.source: We previously reported that H3-G34R mutants also alter the kinetics of phosphorylation at residues S128/129 of histone H2A (Yadav et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: The G34R and G34K mutant H3s may influence signaling through multiple phosphorylation sites clustered on the C-terminus of H2A.
claims.source: Together with our new finding that H3-G34R/K mutants influence the localization of Sgo2, these data suggest the possibility that the G34R and G34K mutant H3s influence signaling through multiple phosphorylation sites clustered on the C-terminus of H2A.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claims.claim: The C-terminus of H2A lies close to the site of G34 substitutions on the H3 N-terminal tail.
claims.source: This is consistent with structural analyses of nucleosomes showing that the C-terminus of H2A lies close to the site of G34 substitutions on the H3 N-terminal tail (Du and Briggs, 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: The homolog of Sgo2, SGO1 in budding yeast has been shown to bind histone H3.
claims.source: We note that an interesting functional link between H3 and Shugoshin has also been made in budding yeast, where the homolog of Sgo2, SGO1 has been shown to bind histone H3.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about budding yeast.

claims.claim: SGO1 binds a 'tension-sensing motif' at residues 42–45 on H3, which is necessary for Sgo1 recruitment to centromeres and for efficient chromosome segregation during mitosis.
claims.source: Although not reliant on G34 or K36 residues of H3, SGO1 binds a 'tension-sensing motif' at residues 42–45 on H3, which is necessary for Sgo1 recruitment to centromeres and for efficient chromosome segregation during mitosis (Deng and Kuo, 2018; Luo et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: The histone acetyltransferase Gcn5 is important for ensuring efficient chromosome segregation when the tension sensing motif is damaged in budding yeast.
claims.source: Intriguingly in this system, the histone acetyltransferase Gcn5 is important for ensuring efficient chromosome segregation when the tension sensing motif is damaged (Buehl et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: H3.3G34 mutants in mammalian cells exert profound transcriptional effects through modulation of Polycomb activity.
claims.source: In keeping with the importance of transcriptional regulation in H3-G34 mutant cells, very recent work from the Lewis lab indicates that H3.3G34 mutants in mammalian cells exert profound transcriptional effects through modulation of Polycomb activity (Jain et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: The decrease in K36me3 on H3.3 G34 mutant histone enhances PRC2 activity to promote elevated H3.3K27me3 in cis on the H3.3 tail.
claims.source: They found that the decrease in K36me3 on H3.3 G34 mutant histone enhances PRC2 activity to promote elevated H3.3K27me3 in cis on the H3.3 tail (Jain et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: Tumorigenesis driven by H3.3G34 mutations derives from enhanced Polycomb-mediated silencing of enhancers of genes that regulate differentiation, whereby cells retain a more stem cell-like fate.
claims.source: They propose that tumorigenesis driven by H3.3G34 mutations derives from enhanced Polycomb-mediated silencing of enhancers of genes that regulate differentiation, whereby cells retain a more stem cell-like fate.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on a proposal from published literature.

claims.claim: Acetylation at enhancers principally resides on K27 of histone H3.3.
claims.source: Since acetylation at enhancers principally resides on K27 of histone H3.3 (Martire et al., 2019), this may explain why the G34 mutations identified in cancer occur solely on H3.3 (Behjati et al., 2013; Schwartzentruber et al., 2012).

claims.source: Phosphorylation of Ser31 in H3.3 is important for regulation of cell fate during gastrulation and for enhancer activation (Martire et al., 2019; Sitbon et al., 2020) and Ser31P influences H3.3 K27 trimethylation and acetylation (Martire et al., 2019; Sitbon et al., 2020), and so phosphoregulation via S31 may provide an additional mechanistic link as to why the Gly 34 mutations are only found in H3.3.

claims.source: Although fission yeast provides an exquisite system for analysis of histone mutations, we fully acknowledge the limitation of work in a system that lacks a Polycomb silencing pathway.

results.result: H3K36me3 is reduced in both H3-G34V and H3-G34R mutants, while H3K36me2 accumulates in both strains.
results.evaluation: Claims C34, C52, C55, and C65 are supported by western blot data in Figure 1C showing marked reduction in H3K36me3 in both G34V and G34R mutants compared to wild-type, with accumulation of H3K36me2. The antibody recognition controls (C53, C54) provide additional validation of the measurements.

results.result: H3-G34R but not H3-G34V mutants show defective H3K36 acetylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C35, C62, C63, and C64 are supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 1D) and in vitro acetylation assays (Figure 1F) showing that H3K36ac is greatly reduced in H3-G34R but unaffected in H3-G34V cells. This represents a key phenotypic difference between the two glioma-associated mutations.

results.result: Gcn5 is the major H3K36 acetyltransferase in fission yeast, and its activity is specifically lost at K36 on G34R H3 in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 and C187-C188 are supported by genetic data (Figure 1E) showing gcn5Δ cells have low H3K36ac, and in vitro acetylation assays (Figure 1F) demonstrating that Gcn5 acetylates K36 on WT H3 but activity is strongly reduced on G34R H3 and slowed on G34V H3. The specificity for K36 while other sites remain unaffected strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: H3-G34R and set2Δ cells are sensitive to multiple forms of replicative stress (HU, MMS, CPT), while H3-G34V cells are not.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C83 are supported by serial dilution growth assays (Figure 2A) showing that H3-G34R and set2Δ cells are sensitive to hydroxyurea, methyl methanesulfonate, and camptothecin, whereas H3-G34V cells show no sensitivity to these agents. This demonstrates distinct DNA damage response profiles between G34R and G34V mutants.

results.result: H3-G34V but not H3-G34R mutants are sensitive to γ-irradiation and IR mimetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C90 are supported by γ-irradiation viability assays (Figure 2B) and serial dilution assays with bleomycin and zeocin (Figure 2C) showing that H3-G34V and set2Δ cells are sensitive to IR and IR mimetics, while H3-G34R cells are not. This represents another key phenotypic distinction between the two glioma mutations.

results.result: H3-G34V cells are proficient for homologous recombination while H3-G34R cells are defective for HR.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C97 are supported by HR efficiency assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and epistasis analysis with rad51Δ (Figure 2D). The epistasis data showing that rad51Δ H3-G34V double mutants are more sensitive than either single mutant, while rad51Δ H3-G34R double mutants are no more sensitive than rad51Δ alone, provides strong genetic evidence for HR proficiency in G34V and deficiency in G34R.

results.result: H3-G34R cells exhibit elevated chromosome loss and missegregation, while H3-G34V cells show genomic stability similar to wild-type.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C103 and C105 are supported by minichromosome loss assays (Figure 2E) showing H3-G34R cells lose Ch16 at 4.3% frequency compared to 1.2% for WT and 2.2% for G34V, and chromosome missegregation assays (Figure 2F) showing 7.4% lagging chromosomes in G34R versus 0.5% in both WT and G34V. This demonstrates distinct genomic stability profiles.

results.result: H3K36me3 is specifically reduced in H3-G34K, G34R, and G34V mutants, but not in G34W, G34M, or G34Q mutants, while H3K36me2 is elevated in all G34 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 are supported by western blot analysis (Figure 3C) of a panel of G34 mutants showing that only mutations introducing basic charges (K, R) or valine reduce H3K36me3, while bulky uncharged (W, M) or negatively charged (Q) substitutions do not. The elevation of H3K36me2 in all mutants (accounting for antibody recognition differences) suggests a defect in the di- to tri-methylation transition.

results.result: Among H3-G34 mutants, only G34R is sensitive to hydroxyurea, while both G34R and G34K (basic substitutions) are sensitive to MMS and CPT, but G34W, G34M, and G34Q are not.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C112 are supported by serial dilution assays (Figure 3D) showing distinct DNA damage sensitivity patterns. The observation that alkylation sensitivity correlates with basic charge rather than size of substitution (C112) is a reasonable inference from the data, though the mechanism remains unclear.

results.result: H3-G34K and H3-G34V mutants are sensitive to γ-IR and IR mimetics, with G34K showing greater sensitivity than G34V or set2Δ, while G34R, G34M, G34W, and G34Q are not sensitive.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C116 are supported by serial dilution assays with bleomycin and zeocin (Figure 3E) and γ-irradiation viability assays (Figure 3F). The data clearly show that G34K and G34V share IR sensitivity, distinguishing them from G34R, and that G34K is more sensitive than either set2Δ or G34V.

results.result: H3-G34K and H3-G34R mutants exhibit elevated chromosome missegregation, but only G34R is defective for HR, as demonstrated by epistasis analysis with rad51Δ.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C121, C123-C125, and C128 are supported by chromosome missegregation assays (Figure 3G) showing elevated lagging chromosomes in G34K (7.4%) and G34R (5.9%) but not other mutants, and epistasis analysis (Figure 3H-I) showing that G34K rad51Δ double mutants are more sensitive than either single mutant while G34R rad51Δ are not. This demonstrates that chromosome missegregation can occur independently of HR defects.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis reveals distinct transcriptional profiles for H3-G34R, G34K, and G34V mutants, with differential regulation of subtelomeric (ST) domains: repression in G34R, slight repression in G34K, upregulation in set2Δ, and WT-like profile in G34V.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C137 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 4A-B, Supplementary file 4) showing that set2Δ has the most differentially expressed genes (478 total), while G34 mutants show fewer changes (160 for G34R, 223 for G34K, 183 for G34V) with only 44 genes misregulated in all three G34 mutants. The distinct ST domain transcriptional profiles are clearly shown in Manhattan plots and validated by RT-PCR.

results.result: Genes downregulated in both G34R and G34K strains are preferentially located in ST domains, and this downregulation is mirrored in cells lacking the H3K36 acetyltransferases Gcn5 and Mst2.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C142 are supported by RNA-seq analysis showing 16/31 downregulated genes in both G34R and G34K are in ST domains versus only 2/29 upregulated genes, and by data showing that gcn5Δmst2Δ cells also show ST domain repression (Figure 4D-E). This links H3K36 acetylation to ST domain transcriptional regulation.

results.result: H3-G34R cells show elevated subtelomeric 'knob' formation and accumulation of Sgo2 at ST domains, correlating with enhanced silencing; this is mirrored in gcn5Δmst2Δ cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C149, C151-C153, and C158 are supported by 3D-SIM microscopy showing increased knobs in G34R but not G34V cells (Figure 5A-B), and ChIP data showing Sgo2-FLAG enrichment at ST domains in G34R compared to G34V or WT (Figure 5C) and in gcn5Δmst2Δ cells (Figure 5D). The correlation between Sgo2 accumulation, knob formation, and ST silencing is well-supported.

results.result: Sgo2 accumulation at centromeres in mitosis is unaffected by H3-G34R mutation, but Sgo2 is preferentially enriched at ST domains even in mitotically arrested G34R cells, suggesting perturbed cell cycle regulation of Sgo2 localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C157 are supported by ChIP data (Figure 5E-F) showing that Sgo2 levels at centromeres are similar between G34R and WT in mitotic cells, but Sgo2 is enriched at ST domains in G34R even during mitotic arrest. The inference about perturbed cell cycle regulation (C157) is reasonable given the data, though the mechanism remains unclear.

results.result: H3-G34K cells show elevated Sgo2 at ST domains, consistent with the pattern seen in G34R and H3K36ac-deficient cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C159 is supported by ChIP data (Figure 5G) showing Sgo2-FLAG enrichment at ST domains in G34K cells. This extends the correlation between basic substitutions at G34, reduced H3K36ac, ST domain silencing, and Sgo2 accumulation.

results.result: Co-expression of wild-type H3 with G34R, G34V, or G34K mutants does not affect global H3K36me3 or H3K36me2 levels, and loss of H3K36ac is restricted to the G34R mutant protein.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C164 are supported by western blot data (Figure 6A) showing no change in H3K36me3 or H3K36me2 in mixed copy strains, and mass spectrometry data (Figure 6B) showing K36ac is present on WT H3 but absent on G34R H3 in mixed copy strains. This demonstrates that K36 methylation and acetylation effects are cis-acting on the mutant histone tail.

results.result: Most DNA damage sensitivities and chromosome missegregation are rescued in mixed copy strains, but H3-G34R (3xH3) retains dominant HU sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C167 are supported by serial dilution assays (Figure 6C-D) showing that mixed copy G34K and G34V strains grow like WT on bleomycin and zeocin, but G34R (3xH3) retains HU sensitivity, and chromosome missegregation assays (Figure 6E) showing no increased lagging chromosomes in mixed copy G34K or G34R strains. This demonstrates that most phenotypes are recessive but HU sensitivity in G34R is dominant.

results.result: H3-G34R mixed copy strains show a significant reduction in HR efficiency compared to wild-type.
results.evaluation: Claim C168 is supported by HR assay data (Figure 6F) showing reduced efficiency in G34R (3xH3) strains. This demonstrates that HR defects in G34R show partial dominance, consistent with the dominant HU sensitivity.

results.result: The number of differentially expressed genes is reduced in mixed copy strains compared to sole copy strains, but ST domain repression is maintained in G34R and G34K mixed copy strains, demonstrating dominant transcriptional effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C169-C177 are supported by RNA-seq data showing fewer differentially expressed genes in mixed copy strains (54 for G34R [3xH3] vs 160 for sole copy G34R), but Manhattan plots (Figure 6G) and RT-PCR (Figure 6H) show ST domain repression is maintained in mixed copy G34R and G34K strains. The enrichment of ST domain genes among repressed genes (10/30 for G34R, 25/69 for G34K) versus activated genes (1/24, 7/73) supports dominant ST silencing.

results.result: The sensitivity of H3-G34R cells to replicative stress cannot be attributed to reduction in H3K36me3 but may be due to loss of H3K36ac.
results.evaluation: Claim C84 is supported by the observation that both G34R and G34V have reduced H3K36me3 (C55, C65) but only G34R shows replicative stress sensitivity (C76-C83) and only G34R has reduced H3K36ac (C62-C64). The inference that H3K36ac loss may cause replicative stress sensitivity is reasonable, though causality is not definitively established.

results.result: All three mutants (G34R, G34V, G34K) with reduced K36me3 show enhanced DNA damage sensitivity, suggesting K36me3 plays a critical role in genome protection, but sensitivity to specific DNA-damaging agents is influenced by additional factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C119 are supported by the observation that G34R, G34V, and G34K all have reduced K36me3 (C106) and all show some form of DNA damage sensitivity (though to different agents), while mutants without K36me3 reduction (G34W, G34M, G34Q) show no DNA damage sensitivity. The inference that additional factors influence specific sensitivities is reasonable given the non-overlapping damage sensitivity profiles.

results.result: The mechanism of reduced H3K36me3 in G34V/R mutants remains unclear; Set2 association with chromatin is unchanged, and loss of the demethylase Epe1 does not affect K36 methylation levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C60 present speculative hypotheses (C57, C58) about defective Set2 trimethylation or heightened demethylase activity, but the experimental tests (ChIP for Set2, C59; deletion of epe1, C60) do not support either mechanism. The claims acknowledge uncertainty but do not provide a definitive mechanism for the K36me3 reduction.

results.result: The HR defect in G34R cells may be linked to loss of H3K36ac, but causality remains unclear despite in vitro evidence that G34R directly affects Gcn5 function.
results.evaluation: Claims C185-C186 and C189 are supported by correlative evidence (both G34R and gcn5 mutants have reduced H3K36ac, HU sensitivity, and HR defects), and C189 is supported by in vitro data showing G34R blocks Gcn5 activity at K36. However, C190 correctly acknowledges that causality is not established, and C191 presents a speculative model for dominant effects. The inability to test causality directly (mentioned in text) limits the strength of this conclusion.

results.result: No evidence was found for arginine methylation of H3-G34R in fission yeast, ruling out this potential mechanism for unique G34R phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C193-C194 are supported by mass spectrometry data (cited as Lowe et al., 2019) showing no methylation of H3-G34R. This negative result is important for ruling out one potential mechanism, though it does not explain the unique G34R phenotypes.

results.result: Local chromatin perturbation from mutant histone deposition is insufficient to cause IR sensitivity in the presence of wild-type H3.
results.evaluation: Claim C195 is supported by the observation that G34V and G34K sole copy strains are IR-sensitive (C87, C115) but mixed copy strains are not (C166). This inference about local versus global effects is reasonable given the data, though the exact mechanism remains unclear.

results.result: Elevated Sgo2 at ST domains in G34R/G34K mutants may delay replication timing or perturb centromere function, potentially explaining chromosome missegregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C200-C201 present speculative hypotheses about mechanisms linking Sgo2 accumulation to chromosome missegregation. While the correlation between Sgo2 accumulation and chromosome defects is established, these mechanistic proposals are not directly tested and remain speculative. The observation that ST silencing is maintained while chromosome missegregation is corrected in mixed copy strains (C202) complicates these models.

results.result: G34R and G34K mutant H3s may influence signaling through multiple phosphorylation sites on the C-terminus of H2A.
results.evaluation: Claim C206 is based on inference from the observation that G34R/K mutants affect Sgo2 localization (which depends on H2A phosphorylation) and previous data showing G34R affects H2A S128/129 phosphorylation kinetics (C205). While the structural proximity of H3 G34 to H2A C-terminus (C207) supports this possibility, the mechanism is not directly tested and remains speculative.

results.result: Previous work showed that H3-G34R mutants have reduced H3K36 trimethylation and acetylation, increased genomic instability and replicative stress, defective HR, upregulation of antisense transcripts, and enhanced subtelomeric silencing.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C27-C31 reference previous work (Yadav et al., 2017) that is validated and extended by data in the current manuscript. The current study confirms these findings and provides mechanistic insights into the differences between G34R and other G34 mutations.

results.result: Recent work shows SETD2 activity is blocked on G34 mutant nucleosomes while NSD2 di-methylation is unaffected; differences from the current study may reflect species differences in H3 sequence or enzyme specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C182 discuss recent published work (Jain et al., 2020) and note discrepancies with the current study (G34W affects tri-methylation in that study but not here). The authors provide reasonable explanations for these differences (C180: fission yeast H3 differs from H3.3 at residues 28 and 31), and the observation that mixed copy strains show no global K36me3 reduction (C181) is consistent with both studies.

results.result: Recent work shows that H3.3 G34 mutants in mammalian cells affect transcription through Polycomb modulation, with decreased K36me3 enhancing PRC2 activity and K27me3, potentially explaining why G34 mutations occur specifically in H3.3.
results.evaluation: Claims C211-C215 accurately summarize recent published work (Jain et al., 2020; Martire et al., 2019) and provide context for understanding why G34 mutations are found specifically in H3.3 in cancer. These claims are appropriately cited and provide important discussion context, though they are not directly tested in the current study.
